system: You are a careful experimenter. You can only use the tools you are given. Numerical results depend on the time step dt: check that a result has converged before you trust it. Report your conclusion in plain text and give the evidence for it.
task: A tennis ball is thrown at 25 m/s from the ground, with air drag. Find the launch angle, to within one degree, at which it lands furthest away, and say by how much that range exceeds the range at 45 degrees. Use as few simulation runs as you can.

steps.text: I will start with the vacuum range at 45 degrees as a reference, and scan the angle with drag at a coarse step dt = 0.01 s: 35, 40 and 45 degrees.

The range peaks near 40 degrees; a parabola through 35, 40 and 45 degrees puts the maximum near 40.5. But these values depend on dt, so I repeat 40, 41 and 45 degrees at dt = 0.002 s before I trust them.

Going from dt = 0.01 to 0.002 s moved the range at 40 degrees by about 0.05 m, so the coarse step was not converged. The ranges at 40 and 41 degrees now agree to 0.001 m, which puts the maximum between them. I check convergence once more at the smallest allowed step, dt = 0.001 s, for 40, 41 and 45 degrees.

Conclusion: the best launch angle is between 40 and 41 degrees, about 40.5, with a range of about 35.73 m. Evidence: at dt = 0.001 s the ranges are 35.7315 m at 40 degrees and 35.7328 m at 41 degrees, and they differ by under 0.002 m, so the maximum lies between them; a parabola through 35, 40 and 45 degrees at dt = 0.01 s gave 40.5 as well. The time step has nearly converged: from dt = 0.002 s to 0.001 s the range changed by 0.006 m at 40 degrees and 0.005 m at 45 degrees, against 0.05 m from 0.01 s to 0.002 s. At 45 degrees the range is 35.403 m, so the best angle lands the ball about 0.33 m (0.9 per cent) further. Without drag the best angle would be 45 degrees and the range 63.7 m, so drag lowers the best angle and nearly halves the range.
